title: Selectivity
description: Measure predicate fractions, distinguish distinct-value ratios, diagnose skew and correlation, and interpret index choices with actual counts and estimates.

questions.question_text: How is selectivity typically calculated?
options: Total number of rows divided by number of distinct values
Number of distinct values divided by total number of rows
Number of indexes divided by number of tables
Number of columns divided by number of rows
questions.explanation: Selectivity = distinct values / total rows — a ratio describing how much a value narrows down the search.

questions.question_text: Which column in the 1, 000, 000-row students table has the HIGHEST selectivity?
options: is_active (boolean, 2 values)
department (20 distinct values)
email (nearly all unique values)
A constant column with only 1 possible value
questions.explanation: email, being nearly unique per row, has selectivity close to 1.0 — the highest among these options.

questions.question_text: Why is a boolean column like is_active generally a poor index candidate?
options: Booleans cannot be stored in indexes
It has only 2 distinct values, so filtering on it still leaves a large fraction of rows matching, providing low selectivity
Boolean indexes are always corrupted
Booleans require a hash index specifically
questions.explanation: A roughly balanced boolean predicate often selects a large fraction, but a rare boolean value under skew can be highly selective. Evaluate the queried value’s distribution rather than distinct count alone.

questions.question_text: In a scenario where a WHERE clause on an indexed column still matches 70% of the table's rows, what is the likely consequence?
options: The index will always be dramatically faster than a full scan
A full table scan may actually be cheaper, since the index-plus-lookups approach would still touch most of the table via scattered I/O
The query will fail to execute
The column's data type is invalid for indexing
questions.explanation: When selectivity is low and most rows match, following many index pointers (random I/O) can be more expensive than a straightforward sequential full scan.

questions.question_text: What does it mean if a column has selectivity close to 1.0?
options: Almost all rows have the same value
Most values are unique or near-unique, so filtering on that column narrows results down sharply
The column cannot be indexed
The column has exactly one distinct value
questions.explanation: Selectivity near 1.0 indicates values are close to unique across rows, meaning filtering narrows the result set dramatically.

questions.question_text: Why can a single overall selectivity number for `department` be misleading if the data distribution is skewed?
options: Selectivity is never misleading under any circumstances
If one department has 80% of all rows and 19 others share the rest, filtering to the big department is low-value even though the average selectivity number looks reasonable
Skewed data makes selectivity impossible to calculate at all
Selectivity can only be computed for numeric columns
questions.explanation: A skewed distribution means the overall average selectivity doesn't reflect the very different real selectivity of filtering to a huge group versus a tiny one — this is why optimizers use histograms for more nuance.

questions.question_text: What statistical tool do real query optimizers often use beyond a single selectivity ratio to handle skewed data distributions?
options: Histograms of value frequency distribution
A random number generator
A separate hash index just for statistics
They ignore skew entirely and always trust the average ratio
questions.explanation: Optimizers commonly maintain histograms capturing how values are distributed, which handles skew better than one single average ratio.

questions.question_text: How is selectivity mathematically related to cardinality (covered in 20.13)?
options: They are unrelated concepts
Selectivity = cardinality (distinct values) divided by total number of rows
Cardinality = selectivity multiplied by the number of indexes
Selectivity and cardinality are always equal to each other
questions.explanation: Selectivity is directly derived from cardinality: selectivity = cardinality / total rows, tying the two concepts together.

questions.question_text: A predicate matches 10 of 10000 rows. What is its observed selected fraction?
questions.explanation: Divide matching rows by total rows.

questions.question_text: Why state the selectivity convention explicitly?
options: SQL forbids the word selectivity
Predicate fraction and distinct-value ratio use different directions
Every engine uses identical terminology
It determines primary key names
questions.explanation: A small predicate fraction and a large distinct ratio can both be called selective.

questions.question_text: A status column has three values, with disputed on one percent of rows. Can disputed still be selective?
options: No, three values makes all filters identical
Yes
Only if NULL is prohibited
Only if all statuses have equal counts
questions.explanation: Specific value frequency matters even with low distinct count.

questions.question_text: What does multiplying predicate fractions assume?
options: A unique primary key
No table exists
Independence of the conditions
Every value is NULL
questions.explanation: Correlated attributes can violate the multiplication assumption.

questions.question_text: Why is index metadata cardinality unsuitable as a uniqueness guarantee?
options: It always counts zero rows
It stores application passwords
It measures only text length
It is an estimate rather than an enforced constraint
questions.explanation: Uniqueness requires a constraint, not a statistics estimate.

questions.question_text: Which can make a broad qualifying range cheaper to read through an index?
options: The index covers the query
Every column is unindexed
The query uses a longer alias
The result is printed in blue
questions.explanation: Coverage can avoid additional full-row retrieval.

questions.question_text: What happens to a matching fraction if five matches are added to 100 rows with five existing matches?
options: It becomes exactly 10/100
It becomes 10/105
It remains 5/100
It becomes 5/105
questions.explanation: Both numerator and denominator increase.

questions.question_text: Which predicate finds missing values?
options: = NULL
> NULL
IS NULL
IN (NULL) always
questions.explanation: Ordinary comparisons with null do not become true.

questions.question_text: Does low matching fraction alone guarantee a fast query?
options: Yes, always
Only on tables without rows
Only if COUNT(*) is omitted
No; a useful access path and workload costs still matter
questions.explanation: The engine may still need to examine many rows.

questions.question_text: Why test both rare and common parameter values?
options: They can have very different result sizes and costs
Parameters always have identical distributions
It changes SQL syntax
It disables constraints
questions.explanation: Skew affects plan suitability.

questions.question_text: What should be preserved during a date-filter rewrite?
options: Only the query character count
Boundary and time-zone semantics
The exact alias spelling only
An arbitrary output count
questions.explanation: Performance changes must preserve the result contract.

questions.question_text: What evidence distinguishes estimated from observed selectivity?
options: The view name versus its alias
SQL comments versus indentation
EXPLAIN estimates versus actual matching and total counts
Index names versus table names
questions.explanation: A plan prediction and measured result population are separate observations.

notes:
## Measure how much a predicate keeps

Predicate selectivity is the fraction of input rows that satisfy a condition. If a campus loan table has ten thousand rows and member_id=7 selects ten, the predicate's observed selectivity is one thousandth. A small selected fraction is often described informally as highly selective. Always state the convention, because index discussions also use selectivity to mean a distinct value ratio, where larger numbers suggest more discrimination.

These two uses answer related but different questions. The distinct ratio describes a column or key population; a predicate fraction describes a particular filter on particular values. A status column can have few distinct values while one rare status is highly selective. Assuming every value occurs equally often can make both human expectations and optimizer estimates misleading.

## A skewed campus example

Imagine ten thousand loans: nine thousand are returned, nine hundred are active, and one hundred are disputed. The distinct status count is three regardless of those frequencies. Filtering disputed selects one percent of rows; filtering returned selects ninety percent. An index on status provides the same available structure for both queries, but retrieving most table rows through it may be less attractive than scanning.

```sql
SELECT status,COUNT(*) AS matching_rows
FROM loans GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_rows FROM loans;
```

These queries establish the observed distribution rather than relying on a guessed average. Divide each matching count by the total to obtain a predicate fraction. Use a decimal expression when writing the calculation so integer arithmetic does not truncate small fractions to zero. Decide what an empty table should report, because division by a zero denominator is not a meaningful selectivity measurement.

## Column cardinality is not join cardinality

Column cardinality often means the number of distinct values. A unique nonnull loan identifier has as many distinct values as rows and supports precise equality lookups. A member identifier repeats across loans, so its distinct count is lower. Neither number alone tells you the final row count of a join, which depends on how matching occurrences appear on both sides.

An index cardinality shown by database metadata is usually an estimate rather than a fresh exact COUNT(DISTINCT column). It can reflect sampled statistics and may change after statistics maintenance. Do not use it as an integrity check for uniqueness. Only an appropriate enforced constraint establishes that duplicate key values are prohibited under the engine's rules.

## Estimates guide access path decisions

The optimizer uses statistics to estimate how many rows each condition retains and compare possible plans. It must consider the cost of reading index entries, retrieving missing row values, applying remaining filters, and joining intermediate results. A selective predicate can reduce work substantially, but no single selectivity threshold guarantees that an index is always preferable.

Coverage changes the tradeoff. An index that contains everything needed by a query may support an efficient index scan even when many rows qualify. A noncovering lookup can require many additional clustered row fetches. Table size, row width, caching, ordering requirements, and the storage engine also matter. Explain the whole access pattern rather than reducing the decision to a slogan about low cardinality columns.

## Several predicates can be correlated

Suppose twenty percent of students belong to the science faculty and twenty percent attend the north campus. Multiplying those fractions predicts four percent for both conditions only under an independence assumption. If every science student attends north campus, the combined fraction is twenty percent instead. If no science students attend north campus, it is zero.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS both_count FROM students
WHERE faculty='Science' AND campus='North';
```

Measure the combined condition directly on a safe representative dataset when investigating an estimate error. A composite index can provide an access path aligned with several predicates, but creating one does not automatically solve every correlation estimate. Separate the question of finding qualifying rows from the question of predicting how many rows qualify.

## Ranges, nulls, and searchable expressions

A due date range can be very selective for a quiet day and broad for an entire year. The same parameterized query can face different optimal strategies for different parameter values. Test common values and rare values rather than validating only one convenient example. A workload with uneven distributions needs evidence across that distribution.

Ordinary equality with null does not select missing values; IS NULL does. COUNT(column) and COUNT(*) also measure different populations when nulls are present. When computing a distinct ratio, state whether missing values are included as a category or excluded from the numerator. Without that definition, two reported selectivity numbers can disagree while both follow their own conventions correctly.

A predicate can select few rows but still be difficult to navigate with a plain column index. Applying a function to every stored value may prevent a straightforward range lookup in that index. For date filtering, a half open interval on the stored datetime often expresses the same calendar day more directly than wrapping every row in a formatting function. Verify equivalence for time zones and boundary rules before rewriting.

## Worked lab: exact fractions

Create a safe local fixture with one hundred loan rows: eighty returned, fifteen active, and five disputed. The observed fractions are 0.80, 0.15, and 0.05. Predict those values before querying. Add another five disputed loans and recalculate using the new total of one hundred and five; the disputed fraction is now ten divided by one hundred and five, not ten percent exactly.

The changing denominator is important when interpreting monitoring results. A count increase alone does not tell you whether a predicate became more or less selective. Compare both numerator and total population, and preserve the time and filtering scope of the observation. A production sample limited to recent records should not be described as the distribution of the entire historical table.

## Worked lab: compare estimates with observations

Run EXPLAIN for returned and disputed filters on the skewed fixture, both before and after an approved local index experiment. Record chosen access paths and estimated rows. Then run ordinary count queries to obtain actual matching counts. A plan estimate near one third of the table for every status would miss the skew; an accurate estimate should reflect that disputed is much rarer than returned.

MySQL supports statistics maintenance and histogram facilities that can improve estimates for suitable workloads. These are engine specific operational tools with their own syntax and effects. Do not run ANALYZE TABLE on production merely as part of a learning exercise. Inspect the engine version, privileges, existing statistics, and approved operational process before changing statistics or asserting that stale statistics explain a slow query.

## Avoid premature index conclusions

An index on a low distinct count status column can still help a rare status query, a covered report, or a composite pattern. Conversely, an index on a high distinct count column is not useful for every query involving that table. Its ordering must match the available search conditions, and the query's selected population still matters. Index usefulness is tied to a workload rather than an isolated column label.

Keep correctness independent from optimization. Changing a date predicate must preserve inclusivity, null treatment, and time interpretation. Replacing an outer join to reduce estimated rows can remove required students. Adding DISTINCT to reduce observed output can hide a cardinality defect. Good tuning preserves the original result contract while reducing the work required to produce it.

## Review and related study

Record the selectivity convention, measured population, parameter values, actual counts, estimates, and relevant access path. These facts let another engineer reproduce the conclusion. A query returning no rows in one fixture is perfectly selective for that fixture but may still be slow if no useful access path exists. Likewise, a fast tiny-table scan does not prove that a large-table workload needs no index.

Continue with [Non Clustered Index](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/non-clustered-index) for secondary lookup costs, [Join Cardinality](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/join-cardinality) for multiplied result counts, and [Multiple Row Subquery](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/multiple-row-subquery) for predicate semantics. Estimate quality, access strategy, and logical correctness should be assessed together while remaining separate claims with separate evidence.
